items.title: India Inc not passing on gains: PM flags salary, sub-par goods
items.where: Front page lead, continued on page 2 (Dheeraj Mishra)
items.syllabus: GS4 › Ethical concerns and dilemmas in private institutions; corporate governance · GS3 › Industrial policy; effects of liberalisation; Make in India · GS2 › Consumer protection
items.summary: At FICCI's annual convention, the PM said industry had not passed on the corporate tax cut to workers through higher salaries or jobs, and said he was 'ashamed' of sub-par goods sold to Indian consumers.
ideas: Tax relief without sharing: corporate tax cut from 30% to 22%, yet the PM asked whether salaries or headcount had risen.
GS4 · Corporate governance / GS3 · Fiscal policy
A tax cut is a public sacrifice; corporate governance demands that its gains reach workers, not only shareholders.
Quality as an ethical duty: a captive market of 1.4 billion breeds complacency; 'our own people' are entitled to good-quality products.
GS4 · Business ethics / GS2 · Consumer protection
Selling sub-par goods because 'it will sell anyway' treats citizens as captive buyers, not stakeholders.

Self-reliance in an era of 'weaponisation of resources': India imports APIs despite being the 'Pharmacy of the World', exports iron ore but imports finished steel, has bauxite but imports aluminium alloys.
GS3 · Industrial policy / Supply chains
Raw-material exports with value-added imports show the gap between resource wealth and manufacturing depth.
Agriculture neglected by capital: India's share of global agri exports is only 2–2.5% as corporates hesitate to invest.
GS3 · Agriculture and food processing
Corporate investment in processing, procurement and export markets can turn India's farm output into an export identity.
Stakeholder nation: larger firms should lift small ones in quality and scale; a country progresses only when it respects farmers, small entrepreneurs, wealth creators and taxpayers.
GS4 · Values / GS3 · MSMEs
Growth that is shared across farmers, MSMEs and workers is both an economic and an ethical idea of progress.
keywords: Firms answer to workers, consumers and society, not only shareholders
The PM's question on salaries is a call for stakeholder capitalism over shareholder primacy.
Trust owed in return for public concessions such as tax cuts
A tax concession creates a fiduciary duty to society: the benefit is held in trust for wider welfare.
Quality slips when demand is assured
Captive-market complacency erodes quality; competitiveness abroad begins with respect for buyers at home.
Using control of inputs and supply chains as leverage
In an era of weaponisation of resources, import dependence on APIs and alloys is a strategic risk.
Moving from raw exports to finished, high-value goods
Exporting iron ore and importing steel signals the need for value-chain deepening.
data: GS3 · Fiscal policy · GS4 · Corporate governance
Despite the corporate tax cut from 30% to 22%, wage growth has lagged, the PM noted.
India's share of global agricultural exports
India's share of global agri exports is only 2–2.5%, far below its farm output.
examples: a PM asking industry to share tax gains with workers
Modi at FICCI 2026: a PM asking industry to share tax gains with workers.
strength in finished medicines, dependence in ingredients
'Pharmacy of the World' imports APIs: strength in finished medicines, dependence in ingredients.
Iron ore out, steel in: resource wealth without manufacturing depth.
consumer dignity as a business value
GS4 · Business ethics · GS2 · Consumer protection
PM 'ashamed' of sub-par goods: consumer dignity as a business value.
pyqs: Moral integrity and professional efficiency in corporate governance.
Is CSR efficient and sufficient for the corporate sector's social role?
CSR makes companies more profitable and sustainable.
Case: food company sells rejected export products in the domestic market.
Satyam scandal and changes in corporate governance.
Companies Act 2013, CSR and inclusive growth.
Corporate lobbies, pluralism and the convergence of wealth and power.

trend.t: Corporate ethics questions began with law and compliance (Companies Act CSR 2013, Satyam 2015), moved to whether CSR pays or suffices (2017, 2022), and then to the character of business itself: moral integrity in corporate governance (2023) and corporate wealth's hold on democracy (GS2, 2026). Case studies (2016, 2018, 2020, 2021, 2024) repeatedly test profit against people: workers, consumers, environment.
trend.watch: CSR and corporate governance recur almost every alternate year in GS4, and 2021's case on selling export rejects at home is the same quality-for-own-citizens issue the PM raised.
focus: Stakeholder vs shareholder model of corporate governance
Fair wages and sharing of gains with workers
Consumer rights and quality as business ethics
Limits of mandated CSR vs voluntary corporate conscience

potential: "Corporate governance is not only about compliance with law but about the moral obligation to share gains with stakeholders." Discuss with reference to recent concerns over wages and product quality. (10 marks)
What ethical issues arise when businesses sell lower-quality products in a captive domestic market? Suggest measures to build a culture of quality. (10 marks)
Examine the ethical responsibilities of industry when it receives public concessions such as tax cuts. (10 marks)

practice.q: "Corporate governance is not only about compliance with law but about the moral obligation to share gains with stakeholders." Discuss with reference to recent concerns over wages and product quality.
parts: Why gains are not shared: challenges

answer.t: Addressing FICCI in November 2026, the PM said industry had not passed on the corporate tax cut (30% to 22%) to workers and was selling sub-par goods at home.

pts.t: A firm draws on workers, consumers and public resources, so it owes them a fair share, not only its shareholders.
pts.ex: PM: 'Have you increased the salaries of your employees?'

pts.t: Tax relief is a sacrifice by the public exchequer; using it only for profit breaks an implicit social contract.
pts.ex: Corporate tax cut to 22% without matching wage gains.

pts.t: Quality is respect for the buyer; a captive market is not a licence for poor goods.
pts.ex: PM: 'Are our own people not entitled to good-quality products?'

pts.k: Integrity over the letter of law
pts.t: Legal minimums such as mandated CSR can coexist with unfair wages; conscience must go further.
pts.ex: Satyam (2009): compliant on paper, fraudulent in substance.

pts.t: Large firms can mentor MSMEs on quality and scale.
pts.ex: PM asks big companies to help smaller ones develop quality.

answer.h: Why gains are not shared: challenges

pts.t: Quarterly profit pressure favours buybacks and dividends over wages.
pts.ex: Tax savings retained as profit, not shared as pay.

pts.t: Abundant labour keeps bargaining power and wages low.
pts.ex: Informal and contract work in manufacturing.

pts.t: Patchy standards and testing let poor goods pass.
pts.ex: GS4-2021 case: export rejects sold domestically.

pts.t: Tie concessions to jobs, wages and quality benchmarks, as in output-linked schemes.
pts.ex: Performance-linked incentive design.

pts.t: Mandatory standards, consumer redress and 'zero defect' as a value.
pts.ex: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 and BIS standards.

pts.t: Boards that measure fair wages and customer trust, not only profit.
pts.ex: Gandhi's idea of trusteeship, recalled by the PM.

answer.t: Good corporate governance is measured by who shares in the gains; profit with fair wages and fair goods is the ethic India's growth needs.

items.title: First SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum opens in New Delhi
items.where: 'PM Modi to open SCO Civilisational Dialogue today' (Divya A, 20 Nov, p. 8); 'Shekhawat: Youth, artists, digital push can preserve shared heritage' (Divya A, 22 Nov, p. 6)
items.syllabus: GS2 › Regional groupings involving India (SCO); India and its neighbourhood · GS1 › Indian culture: art forms, literature and architecture · GS4 › Ethics in international relations; soft power
items.summary: PM Modi inaugurated the first SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum at Purana Qila, with about 20 countries including Pakistan, whose minister attended an official event in Delhi for the first time since Operation Sindoor.
evolution: Modi proposes a dedicated platform for civilisational dialogue at the SCO Summit, Tianjin.
Proposal welcomed in the SCO's Bishkek Declaration.
Modi inaugurates the first SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum at Purana Qila; exhibition 'Astitva' on Delhi's history.
Thematic sessions; 13 ministers speak; Iran proposes three heritage initiatives.
ideas: India's initiative inside the SCO: born of Modi's Tianjin (2025) proposal and welcomed in the Bishkek Declaration, it adds a cultural pillar to a security-heavy grouping.
GS2 · SCO / Groupings
The Civilisational Dialogue Forum gives the SCO a people-to-people pillar beyond security and counter-terrorism.
Heritage as diplomacy: sessions on music, textiles, cuisine, scripts, manuscripts and monastic trails; 'Astitva' traces Delhi's history from 1200 BCE to 1200 CE.
GS1 · Culture / GS2 · Soft power
Shared heritage, from scripts to monastic trails, is soft power that builds trust where politics divides.
Multilateral room for adversaries: Pakistan's minister attended, and Delhi framed it as 'not a bilateral setting', asking all to extend due courtesy.
GS2 · India–Pakistan
Multilateral platforms let India engage Pakistan without changing its bilateral position.
Heritage is also contested: Pakistan has been asserting its Indus claim through Mohenjo-daro and Harappa; its minister invoked Taxila, Gandhara and Ghalib.
GS1 · Indus Valley / GS2 · Neighbourhood
Shared heritage can unite or be claimed; civilisational diplomacy must turn common roots into common ground.
Preserving heritage together: Shekhawat stressed youth, artisans, cultural tourism, digital initiatives and joint research; Iran proposed networks for manuscripts, translation and youth dialogue.
GS1 · Heritage conservation / GS2 · Central Asia
Digitising manuscripts and joint research make heritage a living bridge with Central Asia and West Asia.
keywords: Using shared history and culture to build ties between states
Through the SCO forum, India practises civilisational diplomacy, turning shared heritage into strategic goodwill.
Ministers, scholars and artists together in one dialogue
Bringing ministers and scholars together, the forum blends official and cultural tracks of diplomacy.
Rival national claims over a shared past
The Indus Valley is contested heritage; dialogue can turn it from a claim into a shared legacy.
'The world is one family', the forum's cultural theme
The forum's theme, Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam, frames India's foreign policy as dialogue, not domination.
examples: India's cultural pillar for the SCO
SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum, 2026: India's cultural pillar for the SCO.
Humayun from Central Asia, Sher Shah from Afghanistan: one fort, many roots
Purana Qila: built by Humayun and Sher Shah Suri, a symbol of Delhi's shared Central Asian roots.
dialogue continues on multilateral platforms despite tensions
GS2 · India–Pakistan · GS4 · Ethics in IR
Pakistan minister at the Delhi SCO forum: dialogue survives on multilateral platforms despite tensions.
joint digitisation and translation of shared texts
Iran's proposal to digitise and translate shared manuscripts: heritage conservation through cooperation.
pyqs: Aims and objectives of the SCO; importance for India.
'Virus of Conflict' and the SCO; India's role.
India's relations with the Central Asian Republics.
Soft power (sports, culture) and India–Pakistan goodwill.
Central Asian and Greco-Bactrian elements in Gandhara art.
Ethics and values in Comprehensive National Power, including soft power.

trend.t: SCO questions moved from basics (aims and importance for India, 2021) to its internal frictions (2023's 'virus of conflict'), while Central Asia appeared on its own (2018, 2024). Soft power has been asked as a tool for India–Pakistan goodwill (2015) and as an ethical component of national power (GS4, 2020).
trend.watch: The SCO has come up twice in three years (2021, 2023), and both times the question asked what India can do inside a divided grouping, so India's initiatives within the SCO are a must-study.
focus: India's role and initiatives within the SCO
Cultural and civilisational links with Central Asia
Soft power and people-to-people ties in neighbourhood policy

potential: "Civilisational dialogue can serve as a bridge where political dialogue fails." Discuss in the context of India's initiative within the SCO. (15 marks)
How can shared cultural heritage strengthen India's relations with Central Asia? (10 marks)
Examine the role of soft power in India's engagement with regional groupings. (10 marks)

practice.q: "Civilisational dialogue can serve as a bridge where political dialogue fails." Discuss in the context of India's initiative within the SCO.

answer.t: Proposed by India at the SCO's Tianjin Summit (2025) and welcomed in the Bishkek Declaration, the first SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum opened in New Delhi in November 2026 with about 20 countries, including Pakistan.

pts.t: Shared art, scripts and faith traditions remind states of what unites them beyond current disputes.
pts.ex: Sessions on monastic trails, manuscripts and shared architecture.

pts.t: A multilateral, cultural setting allows engagement without political concessions.
pts.ex: Pakistan's minister attended; Delhi called it 'not a bilateral setting'.

pts.t: Artists, scholars and youth build ties that outlast governments.
pts.ex: Iran's proposed Network for Dialogue Among Youths.

pts.t: A cultural pillar softens a grouping known for counter-terrorism and rivalry.
pts.ex: India's initiative adds culture to the SCO's agenda.

pts.t: History provides a natural bridge to Central Asia where connectivity is limited.
pts.ex: Purana Qila: Humayun from Central Asia, Sher Shah from Afghanistan.

pts.t: Positions India as a civilisational state offering dialogue.
pts.ex: Cultural theme 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam'.

pts.t: A shared past can become a rival claim.
pts.ex: Pakistan asserting its Indus claim through Mohenjo-daro and Harappa.

pts.t: Terrorism and border disputes limit how far goodwill travels.
pts.ex: First Pakistani minister in Delhi since Operation Sindoor; Dargah visit not cleared.

pts.t: China–India and Russia–West tensions shape the SCO's agenda.
pts.ex: GS2-2023: 'virus of conflict' in the SCO.

pts.t: Forums risk becoming photo-ops without follow-up.
pts.ex: Need for institutional networks, not one-off events.

pts.t: States send non-culture ministers, signalling politics over culture.
pts.ex: Pakistan sent its Climate Change minister, not its culture minister.

pts.t: Weak transport and visa links limit exchanges with Central Asia.
pts.ex: Land access to Central Asia blocked through Pakistan.

pts.t: Annual meetings with a secretariat-backed work plan.
pts.ex: Build on the Bishkek Declaration.

pts.t: Digitise and translate shared manuscripts.
pts.ex: Iran's manuscript and translation proposals.

pts.t: Exchanges, scholarships and cultural tourism.
pts.ex: Shekhawat's focus on youth, artisans and digital initiatives.

pts.t: Keep cultural tracks open even when political ties are frozen.
pts.ex: Due courtesy to all delegations at the forum.

pts.t: Pair cultural ties with Chabahar and INSTC links to Central Asia.
pts.ex: India–Central Asia engagement.

pts.t: Joint archaeology and museum exchanges on common sites.
pts.ex: Gandhara and Taxila as shared heritage.

answer.t: As Pakistan's minister said at the forum, 'When history discovers us, it should find that we were talking'; civilisational dialogue keeps that conversation alive while politics catches up.

items.title: Shenzhen Peace Declaration: Trump, Xi, Putin agree on boosting oil supplies, reducing nuclear risks
items.where: Front page, continued on page 2 (AP); editorial 'G3 claims common ground, strikes no bargain' (p. 10); op-eds by Sujan Chinoy and Surupa Gupta (p. 11)
items.syllabus: GS2 › Effect of policies and politics of developed countries on India's interests; important international institutions (UN, ICC) · GS3 › Energy security · GS4 › Ethics in international relations
items.summary: Meeting in Shenzhen on the APEC sidelines, Trump, Xi and Putin agreed to push UN reform, raise refined petroleum supplies, curb the ICC's reach and hold dialogue on nuclear risks.
evolution: Quad leaders meet in Manila; Trump returns to the Quad table before Shenzhen.
Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting.
ideas: Four-point agenda: UN reform, more refined petroleum, curbs on the ICC and 'similar bodies', and dialogue on nuclear risks and proliferation.
GS2 · Great powers / International institutions
The Shenzhen statement shows great powers setting a global agenda outside multilateral institutions.
Common ground, no grand bargain: compared with Yalta (1945), but the Express editorial and Sujan Chinoy see optics over substance, with no breakthrough on Ukraine.
GS2 · World order
Shenzhen is no Yalta: three rivals sought common ground, not a carve-up of the world.
Weakening of rules-based multilateralism: all three leaders prefer personalised, transactional deals over institutions such as the WTO, NATO or the ICC.
GS2 · Multilateralism
Personalised summitry by great powers erodes rules-based multilateralism that protects middle powers.
Accountability bypassed: none of the three is a party to the Rome Statute, and the ICC has a warrant against Putin.
GS2 · International institutions / GS4 · Ethics in IR
Curbing the ICC shields the powerful from accountability, a core ethical concern in international relations.
India's stake: as one of the world's largest refining hubs it gains from steadier fuel supply, but must guard against great-power hegemony through like-minded partnerships and 'strength within'.
GS2 · India's interests / GS3 · Energy security
India's answer to great-power deals is multi-alignment abroad and industrial strength at home.
keywords: Three great powers setting the agenda outside institutions
The Shenzhen troika risks great-power hegemony over rules-based multilateralism.
Arms balance that removes incentives for a first strike
The leaders committed to strategic stability, not to cutting their own arsenals.
Great powers claiming zones of control over smaller states
Russia's call for negotiated spheres of influence threatens the sovereignty of smaller states.
Engaging all powers without joining any bloc
Through multi-alignment, India engages the Quad, ASEAN and the SCO without choosing sides.
data: China's nuclear warheads vs those of the US and Russia
China has over 600 warheads against about 5,000 each for the US and Russia, so it resists arms limits.
examples: GS2 · World order · GS4 · Ethics in IR
Shenzhen trilateral, 2026: great powers bypassing multilateral institutions.
great powers shaping the world order over others' heads
Yalta, 1945: three powers shaped the post-war order over others' heads.
the end of the last US–Russia arms control pact
New START expired in February 2026, ending the last US–Russia nuclear arms pact.
limits of international justice against the powerful
ICC warrant against Putin: limits of international justice against the powerful.
pyqs: UN reform stalled by the USA vs Russo-Chinese alliance.
Economy's challenges as the world moves from multilateralism to protectionism and bilateralism.
India's image as leader of the oppressed in the emerging global order.
BRICS as a counterweight in global governance.
US–Iran nuclear pact controversy and India's interests.
Ethics subjugated to strategic interests in international relations.
Taming the will to power with moral duty in international relations.
Ethical issues in launching and continuing the Russia–Ukraine war.

trend.t: Questions on the world order moved from India's image in a changing order (2019) to great-power rivalry blocking UN reform (2025), the retreat from multilateralism to bilateralism in trade (GS3, 2025) and alternatives such as BRICS (2026). GS4 has paired this with ethics in IR: war (2022), power and moral duty (2020) and strategic interest over ethics (2026).
trend.watch: Great-power rivalry and the decline of multilateralism appeared in both GS2 and GS3 in 2025 and again in 2026, so the shift from rules to power-based deals is a must-study theme across papers.
focus: Decline of multilateralism and great-power deals
UN reform and the role of the P5
Ethics vs power in international relations

potential: "Great-power summitry outside multilateral institutions threatens the rules-based order." Discuss with reference to the recent US–China–Russia trilateral and its implications for India. (15 marks)
"In international relations, power often decides what is just." Examine the ethical issues raised when major powers seek to limit international courts. (10 marks)
How should India navigate a world order shaped by transactional great-power diplomacy? (10 marks)

practice.q: "Great-power summitry outside multilateral institutions threatens the rules-based order." Discuss with reference to the recent US–China–Russia trilateral and its implications for India.
parts: How such summitry threatens the rules-based order
The other side: why it may not

answer.t: On 19 November 2026 in Shenzhen, Trump, Xi and Putin agreed on UN reform, more refined petroleum, curbs on the ICC and dialogue on nuclear risks, prompting comparisons with Yalta (1945).

answer.h: How such summitry threatens the rules-based order

pts.t: Decisions taken by three leaders sideline the UN, WTO and other forums where all states have a voice.
pts.ex: Agenda set at a trilateral, not in the UN General Assembly.

pts.t: Limiting international courts shields powerful states and leaders.
pts.ex: Joint call that the ICC 'must not abuse' its jurisdiction; ICC warrant against Putin.

pts.t: Great-power deals revive the idea that big states decide for small ones.
pts.ex: Russia's argument for negotiated spheres of influence.

pts.t: Leader-to-leader bargains replace stable, rule-based processes.
pts.ex: Surupa Gupta: all three epitomise personalised, transactional leadership.

pts.t: Dialogue replaces binding limits.
pts.ex: New START expired in February; no commitment to cut arsenals.

pts.t: Reform defined by the P5 may freeze out aspirants.
pts.ex: GS2-2025: UN reform stalled by East–West entanglement.

answer.h: The other side: why it may not

pts.t: The three met to find common ground, not to divide the world.
pts.ex: Editorial: 'claims common ground, strikes no bargain'.

pts.t: None can deliver its core aims, limiting real impact.
pts.ex: Sujan Chinoy: 'Shenzhen is no Yalta'.

pts.t: Indo-Pacific states increasingly write their own rules.
pts.ex: ASEAN centrality and multi-alignment on display in Manila.

pts.t: Even talk on nuclear risks lowers the chance of miscalculation.
pts.ex: Commitment to 'strategic stability and international security'.

pts.t: Steadier refined fuel supply helps India as a major refining hub.
pts.ex: Plan to raise refined petroleum output and supply.

pts.t: P5-led reform may sideline India's claim to a permanent seat.
pts.ex: Vague call for 'UN reform' by three P5 members.

pts.t: A US–China thaw can reduce India's weight in US strategy.
pts.ex: Trump–Xi one-on-one in Shenzhen, their third substantial meeting this year.

pts.t: A US–Russia opening may ease pressure on India's Russia links.
pts.ex: Trump–Putin sit-down in Shenzhen.

pts.t: Engage all poles through the Quad, ASEAN, BRICS and the SCO.
pts.ex: India's engagement across Manila forums.

pts.t: Build industrial and technological capacity so others cannot dictate terms.
pts.ex: Editorial: India's ability depends on 'the strength within'.

pts.t: Push inclusive reform of the UN and global finance.
pts.ex: India's voice for the Global South.

pts.t: Partner middle powers to defend rules on trade and the seas.
pts.ex: ASEAN, Japan, Australia.

pts.t: Spread sources and build reserves against supply shocks.
pts.ex: Strategic petroleum reserves.

pts.t: Back institutions that protect smaller states.
pts.ex: Support for UNCLOS and freedom of navigation.

answer.t: Shenzhen shows power seeking to set rules for all; India's answer lies in multi-alignment abroad and strength at home.

ethics.title: Tax cuts, fair wages and the duty to share
ethics.news: The PM told FICCI that industry had not passed on the corporate tax cut to workers and was selling sub-par goods to Indian consumers.
ethics.syllabus: Ethical concerns in private institutions; corporate governance
ethics.link: A tax concession is a public sacrifice; keeping all its gains, underpaying workers and selling poor goods at home breaks the trust between business and society. Stakeholder fairness and quality are corporate governance values, not just economic choices.
ethics.question: "Profit made from public concessions carries a moral duty to workers and consumers." Discuss with reference to corporate governance in India.

ethics.title: Courtesy for an adversary: dialogue at the SCO forum
ethics.news: At the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum in Delhi, India asked all participants to extend due courtesy to Pakistan's delegation, and Pakistan's minister spoke of shared heritage.
ethics.syllabus: Ethics in international relations; tolerance and respect
ethics.link: Extending courtesy to an adversary's delegation shows civility and tolerance without giving up a principled stand on terrorism. Dialogue on shared culture keeps the door to peace open: 'when history discovers us, it should find that we were talking'.
ethics.question: How can cultural dialogue serve as an ethical tool for peace between nations in conflict?

ethics.title: Power above accountability: the Shenzhen call to curb the ICC
ethics.news: Trump, Xi and Putin said the ICC and similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction; none of the three is party to the Rome Statute.
ethics.link: When the most powerful states seek to limit international courts, accountability becomes a rule only for the weak. The ethical test of a world order is whether law binds the strong as well.
ethics.question: "International justice that cannot reach the powerful is not justice." Examine with reference to recent attempts to limit international courts.

essay.title: One fort, many roots
essay.text: At Purana Qila, Pakistan's minister said Delhi 'has not been diminished' by peoples from outside but grew stronger: the fort was begun by Humayun of Central Asia and carried forward by Sher Shah Suri from Afghanistan.
essay.use: For 'South Asian societies are woven not around the state, but around their plural cultures and plural identities' (2019) and 'Culture is what we are, civilization is what we have' (2020).

essay.title: 'Kitna hi khilao, pet bharta nahin'
essay.text: Telling industry it had not shared the tax cut with workers, the PM said: 'aap ki bhookh itni hai, kitna hi khilao pet bharta nahin hai' (your appetite is such that it is never satisfied).
essay.use: For 'Need brings greed, if greed increases it spoils breed' (2016).

essay.title: Power that will not disarm
essay.text: After the Shenzhen trilateral, Trump said 'once you have the nuclear weapons it's very hard to not have them'; the three powers agreed only to dialogue on nuclear risks, not to cut their own arsenals.
essay.use: For 'With greater power comes greater responsibility' (2014).
